section.title: God Is King over All the Earth
section.sectionRationale: An enthronement psalm summoning all peoples, not Israel alone, to celebrate God's universal kingship, its picture of God ascending amid shouts of joy has long been read by the church alongside Christ's own ascension and reign over all nations.
section.thesis: All peoples are summoned to clap and shout for God the great King who reigns over all the earth and gathers the nations to Himself, a psalm fulfilled in Christ's ascension to His throne and the ingathering of the nations as fellow heirs with Abraham's people.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the summons to all peoples to shout for the great King, verses 1-4; God's ascension amid joyful acclamation, verses 5-7; and God's universal reign over the gathered nations, verses 8-9.

units.label: Clap your hands, all you peoples
units.note: the summons to all peoples to shout for the great King

verses.text: Clap your hands, all you peoples; shout unto God with a voice of triumph.
How {{yare|awesome}} is the LORD Most High, the great King over all the earth!
He subdues nations beneath us, and peoples under our feet.
He chooses our inheritance for us, the pride of Jacob, whom He loves. Selah

units.label: God has ascended amid shouts of joy

verses.text: God has {{alah|ascended}} amid shouts of joy, the LORD with the sound of the horn.
Sing praises to God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises!
For God is King of all the earth; sing profound praises to Him.

units.label: God reigns over the nations
units.note: God's universal reign over the gathered nations

verses.text: God reigns over the nations; God is seated on His holy throne.
The nobles of the nations have assembled as the people of the God of Abraham; for the shields of the earth belong to God; He is highly exalted.

yare.gloss: Awesome, to be feared or held in reverent awe. The psalmist uses this word to describe the LORD Most High, the great King whose reign inspires reverence in every people, not Israel alone.

alah.gloss: To go up or ascend. God's ascension amid shouts of joy and the sound of the horn has long been read by the church alongside Psalm 68:18 and Christ's own ascension, quoted in Ephesians 4:8-10.

basic.context: This enthronement psalm summons all peoples, not Israel alone, to clap and shout for God, the great King over all the earth, who has chosen Israel's inheritance and now ascends amid joyful acclamation to His holy throne, gathering the nobles of the nations as the people of the God of Abraham.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm's universal summons, 'all you peoples,' verse 1, and its picture of the nations gathered 'as the people of the God of Abraham,' verse 9, reveal that God's kingship was never meant for Israel alone but always aimed at drawing every nation into worship of the one true King.
basic.originalLanguages: The LORD is called yare, awesome, verse 2, the great King over all the earth. He is pictured as alah, ascending, verse 5, amid shouts of joy and the sound of the horn, language the church has long read alongside Christ's own ascension.
basic.typology: God's ascension amid shouts of joy and the sound of the horn anticipates Christ's ascension to the Father's right hand, celebrated in Acts 1 and interpreted in Ephesians 4:8-10, while the nobles of the nations gathering as Abraham's people anticipates Gentile believers grafted into God's covenant family through faith.
basic.christ: This psalm's picture of God ascending amid triumphant shouts finds its fulfillment in Christ's ascension, Acts 1:9-11, interpreted by Paul in Ephesians 4:8-10 as the King's triumphant rise to give gifts to His church, while the psalm's ingathering of the nations anticipates the church, Jew and Gentile united as Abraham's true offspring, Galatians 3:29.
basic.god: God is shown as the great King over all the earth, not merely Israel's tribal deity, One whose subjugation of nations and choice of inheritance for His people ultimately serves His larger purpose of drawing every nation to worship Him.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 4:8-10 interprets Christ's ascension in the same triumphant, gift-giving terms this psalm's enthronement language anticipates. Acts 1:9-11 records Christ's actual ascension to the Father's right hand. Galatians 3:26-29 shows Gentile believers becoming Abraham's true offspring through faith, fulfilling this psalm's vision of gathered nations.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's summons for every people to shout for God's universal kingship, and its vision of the nations gathered as Abraham's people, finds its fulfillment in Christ's ascension to His throne and in the church, Jew and Gentile together, gathered as the true people of the God of Abraham through faith in Him.

context.literary:
The psalm has two panels, verses 1 to 4 and 5 to 9, and each opens with a summons and closes with a reason. Both panels are stitched together with the small word 'for' (ki) at verses 2 and 7, and both give the same reason: God is King over all the earth. The first panel says it in verse 2, 'the great King over all the earth,' and the second says it in verse 7, 'God is King of all the earth.' The middle of the psalm is therefore a hinge on which the shout swings.

The commands come in a pile: clap, shout, sing praises. Verse 6 has the verb for singing praise four times in a row, a stammer of joy. The psalm's mood is that of a crowd that cannot stop. There are two other bookends. The first and last movements both use the same root for 'exalted' and 'ascended': God 'has ascended' in verse 5, and at the end He is 'highly exalted' in verse 9, a form of the same verb. The psalm begins by summoning a shout and ends with God lifted high, the ascent from beginning to end.

The shape also moves in space. Verse 1 begins with all the peoples on the earth, verse 5 sees God going up, and verse 9 gathers the leaders of the nations round a seated King. It is a psalm with a procession in it: the nations are summoned, God rises, and the nations are brought in to sit at His feet. The heading names the sons of Korah, and the psalm belongs to the small group that follows Psalm 46 and precedes Psalm 48.
context.historical:
Many readers connect the psalm with a festival at which the ark of the covenant, the throne-seat of God's presence, was carried up to the sanctuary on Zion. David's bringing up of the ark is described with 'shouting and the sounding of the ram's horn,' 2 Samuel 6:15, and the chronicler adds trumpets, cymbals and harps, 1 Chronicles 15:28. The words of verse 5 sound so much like that day that the psalm was almost certainly sung in some form of that procession, though the text does not tell us which.

The ancient world knew enthronement festivals for its kings, in which a monarch was acclaimed with shouts and horns, and Israel took over the form and fixed it on the LORD alone. Kings in the region were thought of as owning their land and its gods by conquest. Here the reverse is confessed. The LORD is King over 'all the earth,' and the peoples themselves are invited to clap. The vocabulary of the palace is used to make a claim no palace could make.

There is a strong Jewish tradition that ties this psalm to the new year, when the shofar is sounded, and the psalm is recited seven times before the horn is blown. That practice is later than the psalm, but it fits the mention of the horn and the picture of the LORD as King.

The historical difficulty of the psalm is the last verse. In Israel's actual history the nations were rarely seen gathering to worship. The peoples on the border were more often enemies, and verse 3 speaks of subduing nations. The psalm therefore lived with tension in the days it was sung: the great King was already on His throne, and His subjects had not yet all come.
context.canonical:
The psalm is one of a cluster in the Psalter that proclaim the LORD's kingship, alongside Psalms 93, 96, 97, 98 and 99. Several use the cry 'The LORD reigns,' for example Psalms 93:1 and 99:1. Psalm 47:8 says nearly the same thing with 'God reigns over the nations.' Because Psalm 47 belongs to the part of the Psalter that prefers the name Elohim, that is God, the cry is worded with 'God' where the others say 'LORD.'

The nations are a recurring theme in the neighbouring songs. Psalm 96 tells Israel to declare God's glory among the nations, and Psalm 98:6 uses the same instruments as Psalm 47: 'With trumpets and the blast of the ram's horn shout for joy before the LORD, the King.' Psalm 68:18 addresses God who 'ascended on high' and received gifts, and Paul builds on it, as we shall see. Psalm 22:27-28 also looks to all the ends of the earth turning to the LORD.

The last verse points back to Genesis, since the nations are gathered under the God of Abraham. God had promised Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, and that he would be the father of many nations, Genesis 17:5. Psalm 47:9 is a glimpse of that promise coming home.

The New Testament uses the psalm's themes at three points. The ascension of Christ is described in Luke 24:51 and Acts 1:9-11, and Paul writes of the risen Christ ascending far above all, Ephesians 4:8-10. Paul in Romans 15:9-12 gathers a chain of Old Testament texts about the Gentiles praising God and rejoicing with His people. And the last book pictures a great multitude from every nation standing before the throne, Revelation 7:9-10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wants Israel to see that the God they have been singing to is larger than they had supposed. It is tempting for a small nation to think of its God as a local power, a patron who happens to be theirs. The psalm bursts that idea. In the first verse it invites 'all you peoples' to clap, before Israel is even mentioned, and it insists on the title 'King over all the earth' twice.

At the same time, the psalm does not flatten Israel's place. Verse 4 says God 'chooses our inheritance for us,' and calls Israel 'the pride of Jacob, whom He loves.' The author wants the people to keep both truths together. Their inheritance is a gift, and not an achievement, and their God is not only theirs. Chosen people are not the only people God cares about; they are the people through whom He means to reach the rest.

The psalm also intends to move the worshiper's body. Clapping, shouting and blowing horns are commanded, so that faith is not silent. To the first hearers it was an instruction for a festival and a way of teaching Israel that praise is an act of the whole person. The last thing the author wants them to grasp is that the King's triumph ends not in slaughter but in a gathering: the leaders of the nations 'have assembled as the people of the God of Abraham.' The aim of God's kingship is to have subjects who worship.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes an event, God's going up amid shouts, and a celebration of a rule that is already in force. It does not command Israel to conquer the nations, and verse 3, which says God subdues nations under 'our feet,' has to be read carefully. It is not a licence for anyone to subject other peoples in God's name. The subduing is what God does, in His own time, and by the end of the psalm the picture has changed from subject peoples to worshiping ones.

What the psalm prescribes is worship of a certain kind: loud, joyful, corporate, and open to every people. Believers are told to clap and to sing with understanding, and the footnote to verse 7 offers 'sing a Maskil,' that is, a thoughtful song. Praise is meant to be both glad and informed. It also sets a direction for the church's mission. If all peoples are invited to praise, then a community that keeps this psalm in its songbook cannot shut its doors on the nations. The New Testament draws exactly that conclusion in Romans 15:9-12.

debates.question: Does 'God has ascended' in verse 5 describe a historical liturgical procession, such as the ark being carried up to Zion, or point forward typologically to a future divine ascension?

views.label: The verse describes a historical or liturgical reenactment of the ark of the covenant being carried up into the sanctuary on Mount Zion, the concrete occasion for this psalm's composition
views.case: The sound of the horn and the shouts of joy fit the description elsewhere in Scripture of the ark's procession, 2 Samuel 6:15, suggesting a real liturgical event as the psalm's original setting.

views.label: The verse points forward typologically beyond any ark procession to God's own final ascension and enthronement over all nations, later fulfilled in Christ's ascension
views.case: The psalm's universal scope, God ascending as King 'of all the earth,' verse 7, and gathering 'the nobles of the nations,' verse 9, exceeds what any single ark procession could accomplish, pointing toward a greater fulfillment.

debates.bearing: Whichever original liturgical setting is in view, the church has long read this ascending King as foreshadowing Christ's own ascension and enthronement over all nations, a reading the New Testament's use of similar enthronement psalms, such as Psalm 68, supports.

debates.question: Who are the 'nobles of the nations' in verse 9, and how do they relate to 'the people of the God of Abraham'?

views.label: Converts who join God's people
views.case: The natural sense of the Hebrew is that the nobles have assembled as a people belonging to the God of Abraham, that is, they have been gathered in and now share Abraham's God. Translations differ between 'as' and 'with' the people, because the Hebrew has no separate word for either. On this reading the psalm anticipates the promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham, Genesis 12:3, and the ingathering described in Isaiah 2:2-4.

views.label: Vassals who come to pay homage
views.case: The verse is set after a passage about subduing peoples, and the nobles may simply be the rulers of subdued nations assembling to acknowledge the King, as vassals gathered at a great king's court. The 'shields of the earth,' commonly understood as the rulers who protect the peoples, belong to God, so they surrender their protective power to Him.

views.label: A future hope beyond the psalm's day
views.case: Since the nations had not gathered to worship in the days of Israel's kings, some read the verse as prophetic, a promise which the church sees fulfilled when Gentiles are brought into the family of Abraham through faith, Galatians 3:28-29, and which will be complete when the multitude from every nation stands before the throne, Revelation 7:9-10.

debates.bearing: On any reading the direction of the psalm is toward the nations, and their coming is by God's action. Whether their gathering is voluntary worship or submission, the New Testament sees the fullest sense in Gentile faith in Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
The first command, 'clap your hands,' uses tiqe'u kaf, from a verb that means to strike or blow. It is the verb for blowing a horn and for driving a tent peg. The clap is a strike, a percussive sound rather than a gentle applause. It goes with teru'ah, the 'shout of triumph,' a word that names the battle cry, the alarm blast, and the acclamation given to a king. The same word describes the sound of the horn at the ark's ascent, and it returns in verse 5 in 'shouts of joy.' In Numbers 10:5-6 the same term names the trumpet blasts that set the camp in motion. In the psalm, the shout for God is the noise of Israel going to war turned into the noise of a coronation.

Verse 2 calls the LORD 'awesome,' nora, from a root meaning to fear, so the sense is 'to be feared' or 'inspiring awe.' It is a passive participle: He is the one who is feared. The same verb is used of God's deeds in the exodus, Exodus 15:11, and of His name in the temple. He is called 'Most High,' elyon, and 'great King,' melek gadol, a title used by the emperors of the ancient world for themselves. The psalm claims it for God. It is worth noticing that the psalm gives no name to this King but 'God' and 'LORD,' since His identity does not need a rival to be marked out.

Verse 4 says He 'chooses our inheritance for us.' The word for inheritance, nachalah, is the word for the land as a family portion handed down, a gift that a father assigns and that cannot be earned. The verb 'chooses' is bachar, the word used of God's election of Israel, Deuteronomy 7:6. 'The pride of Jacob' is ge'on Ya'aqov, and here 'pride' is a good thing, the splendour or glory that God gave the land. Elsewhere in the prophets the same phrase can be used bitterly when the people misplace their trust, but in this psalm it is a gift from a loving God, 'whom He loves.'

Verse 5 says God has 'ascended,' alah, the ordinary verb of going up, used for going up to Jerusalem, for climbing a mountain, and for the ark's going up to Zion. The same root appears again in verse 9 as 'highly exalted,' na'alah, a passive form, giving the psalm a bracket of ascent and exaltation. In between is the horn, shofar, the ram's horn, which is not a musical instrument in the modern sense but a signal that announces a king and calls a people to attention.

Verse 8 has 'reigns,' malak, in the form used in the cry 'The LORD reigns' in the enthronement psalms. Some scholars read it as 'has become King,' the moment of accession, and others as 'is King,' a standing state. The verse's picture of God 'seated on His holy throne' suggests He has taken His seat and is now ruling. The word for 'seated,' yashav, is the same word for sitting as king or judge, as in Psalms 9:7. The psalm never says God had to win His throne; it says He sits on it.

typology.type: The ark carried up to Zion amid shouts and horns, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: David's procession with the ark, 2 Samuel 6:15, brought the throne-seat of God to Jerusalem with the very sound the psalm names. The ascension of Jesus is the greater bringing up: He was carried up into heaven as His disciples watched, Luke 24:51 and Acts 1:9-11, and He sits at the right hand of God, Acts 2:33. The ark was a small box placed in a tent, and the enthronement of the Son is in the true sanctuary, Hebrews 9:24. The type falls short because the ark could be lost or captured, as in 1 Samuel 4, while the Son has entered heaven itself and cannot be taken from His throne.

typology.type: The King seated on His holy throne, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: Israel knew a line of kings who reigned from David's throne, and their reigns were partial and often bad. Jesus is the King whom the nations were promised. Peter says David foresaw that God would seat one of his descendants on his throne, and that God has made Jesus both Lord and Christ, Acts 2:30-36. Daniel saw one like a Son of Man given dominion so that every people would serve Him, Daniel 7:13-14. The correspondence is real, the escalation is that this King reigns over all the earth and not only over a small territory, and the type falls short in that earthly kings die and their thrones pass on.

typology.type: Captives and gifts: the ascending King, verse 5 read with Psalm 68:18
typology.fulfillment: The psalm's picture of the ascent leads Paul to Psalm 68:18, which he applies to Christ: He ascended on high, led captives away, and gave gifts to men, Ephesians 4:8. In the psalm the conquering God receives gifts from men, and Paul says the ascended Christ gives gifts to His people, the apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers of Ephesians 4:11. The pattern is that of a victor who takes tribute and then shares the spoil. The psalm's type is unfinished on earth because it was the warrior's triumph without the Spirit-given gifts, which belong to the risen and ascended Lord.

typology.type: The nobles of the nations gathered as the people of Abraham's God, verse 9
typology.fulfillment: The promise made to Abraham was that all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, and the psalm sees the leaders of the nations gathered as his people. Paul says that the Gentiles who believe are Abraham's seed and heirs of the promise, Galatians 3:28-29, and that they have been brought near by the blood of Christ, Ephesians 2:13-19. John sees a multitude from every nation, tribe, people and tongue before the throne, Revelation 7:9-10. The type falls short in that the psalm names nobles only, while the gospel gathers the poor and the slave as well, with no distinction of rank.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by the ascent. The whole of verse 5 is a picture of a King going up to His throne with the sound of the horn, and the New Testament has an event that fits it. Luke ends his Gospel with Jesus blessing His disciples and being carried up into heaven, and the disciples 'worshiped Him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy,' Luke 24:51-53. In Acts they watch Him taken up in a cloud, Acts 1:9-11. The psalm asks the nations to shout at the going up of the King, and the disciples do something like it. It would be wrong to say that the psalm was written only for this event, since the first singers were dealing with the ark, but the church has always heard the ascension in it. Its use in the liturgy of Ascension Day is very old.

It leads to Christ by the meaning of the ascent, which Paul opens up in Ephesians 4:8-10. He quotes Psalm 68:18, a companion psalm about God ascending, and applies it to Christ. The One who ascended is the One who first descended, and He rose 'in order to fill all things.' The ascent is not an escape from the world but the King taking up authority over it. Peter says the same in Acts 2:33: He is exalted to the right hand of God, and has poured out the Spirit. The gifts of Ephesians 4 are the spoil of a victory.

It leads to Christ by the kingship. 'God is King of all the earth' is in the New Testament the confession that Jesus is Lord, Philippians 2:9-11. The psalm cannot be said to name the Messiah, but its picture of a divine King enthroned on a holy throne finds its answer in the One to whom 'all authority in heaven and on earth has been given,' Matthew 28:18. Jesus then sends His disciples to make disciples of all nations, Matthew 28:19, which is exactly the direction of the psalm's first verse.

It leads to Christ by the ingathering. The nobles of verse 9 gather as the people of Abraham's God. Paul teaches that those who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed, Galatians 3:29, and that Christ has made the two, Jew and Gentile, one new people, Ephesians 2:14-19. The great crowd in Revelation 7 is the psalm's last verse at full size.

A word of care keeps the reading honest. The psalm does not mention the Messiah, and the Old Testament context is the ark and the festival. Not every detail should be read as Christ, such as the subduing of nations under Israel's feet, which does not point to military conquest by the church. The links here are those the New Testament itself draws, through the ascension, the enthroned Lord and the Gentile ingathering.
study.god:
The psalm shows God first as King over all. The claim is that Israel's God is not a tribal deity but the Ruler of every people, and the psalm makes the claim twice, at verses 2 and 7. This is a strong doctrine of God's sovereignty, and it is worth noticing that it appears in a song of joy and not a textbook. The kingship that the psalm proclaims is one that the nations are invited to celebrate.

It shows Him as both awesome and near. He is 'the LORD Most High,' and yet He has 'chosen our inheritance' and loves Jacob, verse 4. A King who is only awesome would be feared, and a King who is only loving would not be trusted with a throne. The psalm holds the two together. The love does not shrink the majesty, and the majesty does not cancel the love. The same God who is 'to be feared' has set His love on a people who did nothing to earn it, since Jacob's pride is a gift.

He is a God who moves. The picture of ascent shows God on the way to His throne, and Israel's worship follows Him. The ark is not God's cage, but a sign that He goes before His people and is taken up in their praise. The verse gives no hint that the ascent is a retreat. It is a coronation. Alongside this, He is a God who sits: 'seated on His holy throne,' verse 8. The psalm holds the movement of the procession and the rest of the throne in one view.

He is a God who gathers. The end of the psalm is not the defeat of the nations but their gathering under the God of Abraham. That reveals the purpose behind the subduing: God's sovereignty is not for its own sake but for a worshiping family. The shields of the earth, the protecting powers of the nations, 'belong to God,' which means no ruler holds power in his own right. Every king's authority is on loan, and every throne sits below His.

There is also a tension the psalm leaves open. The God who subdues nations in verse 3 gathers them in verse 9. The hearer must keep both in mind: His rule is real, and it is not cruelty. He is not a partial God, and yet He has His chosen inheritance.

For worship, the psalm teaches the church to make a noise. It gives permission for joy that is loud, and it gives that joy a reason: God reigns. It also gives the church an outward look. A community that has understood who the King is cannot keep Him to itself, and every clap and shout should carry an invitation to those who have not yet been gathered in.

crossReferences.note: David and all Israel bring up the ark with shouting and the sounding of the ram's horn. The words are very close to verse 5, and this scene is the most likely background: the ark, the throne-seat of God, ascends to Zion amid joyful noise.

The chronicler's fuller account adds trumpets, cymbals, harps and lyres to the shouting and rams' horns. It shows the range of sound behind the commands of Psalm 47, and it makes clear that the festival was a national and musical event.

Another enthronement psalm calls for trumpets and the blast of the ram's horn before the LORD, the King. The shared instruments and the shared title show that Psalms 47 and 98 sing the same event of divine kingship, one from the side of the nations and the other from the side of creation.

God ascended on high, led captives, and received gifts from men, and the Lord is in His sanctuary as He was at Sinai. This is the companion picture of the ascending God, and Paul quotes it in Ephesians 4 when speaking of Christ.

The gates are told to lift up their heads so that the King of Glory may enter, and the answer is the LORD of Hosts. It is another psalm of the ark's entry, and it pairs with Psalm 47 to show how Israel sang the arrival of the King.

God promises Abraham that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him. The last verse of the psalm, which names the God of Abraham as the one whose people the nations join, is the promise seen from the far end.

The disciples watch Jesus taken up while a cloud hides Him from sight, and two men promise He will return the same way. This is the event the church most often hears behind the psalm's 'God has ascended.'

Paul quotes Psalm 68:18 and says that the One who ascended is the One who descended, rising above all the heavens to fill all things. He reads the ascent as the King's triumph over enemies and the giving of gifts to His people.

One like a Son of Man approaches the Ancient of Days and is given dominion so that all peoples and nations serve Him. It takes the psalm's picture of the enthroned King over the nations and gives the King a human form.

Paul strings together Old Testament calls for the Gentiles to praise God and rejoice with His people, ending with the Root of Jesse ruling the nations. It shows that the early church read the invitation to all peoples, as in Psalm 47:1, as being fulfilled in Christ.

In Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, and those who belong to Him are Abraham's seed and heirs of the promise. It states the reality behind the nobles of the nations gathering as the people of the God of Abraham.

A multitude too large to count, from every nation, tribe, people and tongue, stands before the throne and cries out salvation to God and to the Lamb. It is the picture of the psalm's ending, with the nations gathered and the King enthroned.

study.oneStory:
The psalm answers a question that begins at Babel: what happens to the scattered nations? In Genesis 11 humanity is broken into peoples and languages, and the story of the Bible turns at once to one man, Abraham, and one promise, that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3. Psalm 47 sings the far side of that promise. The scattered families are called back, and the leaders of the nations are gathered in the presence of the God of Abraham. The blessing that began with one household ends in a great assembly.

It also answers the question about who rules. From the first chapters the Bible has a struggle over dominion, since humanity was made to reign under God, Genesis 1:26-28, and the rebellion of Genesis 3 puts other powers in charge. Israel's kings are a partial answer, and often a failed one. The psalm names the real King who was there all along, and its first verse dares to ask the whole world to acknowledge Him.

The story moves through the ark and the temple. God dwells with Israel in a tent, then in a house, and the ark ascends the hill in a shout. But the prophets say the nations are still outside, and the exile shows that the King's people can be driven away. The psalm therefore waits for something more.

The rest of the Bible supplies it. In Christ the King goes up, having descended to the lowest place, Ephesians 4:9-10, and from His throne He pours out the Spirit and sends His people to every nation, Acts 2:33 and Matthew 28:19. The Gentiles are brought in as Abraham's seed through faith, Galatians 3:29. That is the gathering of verse 9, still in progress.

The end is the new creation, where the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and of His Christ, and He reigns forever, Revelation 11:15. The peoples stream in, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24. The King who ascended will come again as He went, Acts 1:11, and then the clapping of the nations will be the sound of home.

quiz.q: Who is summoned to clap and shout in verse 1?

options.text: All peoples, not Israel alone.
options.note: The psalm's universal summons addresses every people, revealing God's kingship extends beyond Israel.

options.text: Only the priests serving in the temple.
options.note: The summons is explicitly to 'all you peoples,' not a restricted group of priests.

options.text: Only the king and his royal court.
options.note: The call goes out universally to all peoples, not merely to royal officials.

options.text: Only the tribe of Judah.
options.note: The summons reaches beyond any single tribe to all peoples of every nation.

quiz.q: What title does verse 2 give the LORD?

options.text: The great King over all the earth.
options.note: This title establishes God's universal kingship as the psalm's central theme.

options.text: The God of Israel's armies alone.
options.note: The title given is universal, King over all the earth, not restricted to Israel's armies.

options.text: The judge of Israel only.
options.note: The psalm's scope is explicitly universal, King over all the earth, not Israel alone.

options.text: The shepherd of Jacob's flock.
options.note: While God does care for Jacob, verse 2's specific title is King over all the earth.

options.text: God ascends amid shouts of joy and the sound of the horn.
options.note: This ascension imagery has long been read by the church alongside Christ's own triumphant ascension.

options.text: God descends to judge the nations directly.
options.note: The verse describes God ascending, not descending, amid joyful acclamation.

options.text: The ark of the covenant is destroyed by enemies.
options.note: The verse celebrates a triumphant ascension, not destruction or defeat.

options.text: The people mourn the loss of their king.
options.note: The scene is one of joyful shouting and celebration, not mourning.

quiz.q: Who gathers in verse 9 as the people of the God of Abraham?

options.text: The nobles of the nations.
options.note: This pictures nations beyond Israel being drawn into God's own covenant people, anticipating Gentile inclusion in Christ.

options.text: Only the descendants of Isaac and Jacob.
options.note: The text specifically names the nobles of the nations, not merely Israel's own physical descendants.

options.text: The armies defeated in battle.
options.note: The nobles gather in worship and assembly, not as a defeated or subjugated army.

options.text: The priests of foreign religions.
options.note: The nobles gather as worshipers of the one true God, not as representatives of other religions.

quiz.q: What New Testament event does this psalm's ascension language anticipate?

options.text: Christ's ascension to the Father's right hand.
options.note: Acts 1:9-11 and Ephesians 4:8-10 present Christ's ascension in triumphant, kingly terms this psalm anticipates.

options.text: The birth of Christ in Bethlehem.
options.note: The ascension imagery points toward Christ's rising to His throne, not His birth.

options.text: The destruction of the Jerusalem temple.
options.note: The psalm's ascension imagery is triumphant and hopeful, not connected to the temple's destruction.

options.text: The final judgment at the end of the age.
options.note: While God's universal reign does anticipate final judgment, the specific ascension imagery of verse 5 points most directly to Christ's own ascension.

questions: This psalm summons all peoples, not Israel alone, to worship God as King. How does knowing that God's kingship has always aimed at the nations shape your own sense of mission toward people different from you?
God is described as awesome, the great King over all the earth. When was the last time you felt genuine awe, rather than mere familiarity, in worship?
God's ascension amid shouts of joy anticipates Christ's own ascension to His throne. How does picturing Christ enthroned and reigning right now change how you face today's uncertainties?

The nobles of the nations gather as the people of the God of Abraham, verse 9, anticipating Gentile inclusion in Christ. If you came to faith from outside Israel's physical line, how does this psalm's vision deepen your sense of belonging to God's people?

The psalm calls for repeated, enthusiastic praise, 'sing praises, sing praises,' verse 6. What would it look like for your own praise this week to move from routine to genuine celebration of God's reign?

translationNotes.note: Awesome renders yare, describing reverent fear or wonder appropriate before the great King over all the earth, not mere intellectual admiration.
Ascended renders alah, later read by the church at Ascension Day alongside Psalm 68:18 and Ephesians 4:8-10 concerning Christ's own rise to His throne.

The nobles of the nations gathered as the people of the God of Abraham can be read either as foreign rulers submitting to Israel's God or as the nations themselves being joined to Abraham's people; either reading pictures Gentile inclusion in God's worship.
